item.title: TENKi: counting the value of borrowed knowledge to a materials campaign in measurements saved
item.description: Materials campaigns draw on data of very different cost: a band gap costs almost nothing from a database, core-hours from a hybrid-functional density functional theory (DFT) calculation, and instrument time from a measurement. No calibration carries values from low-cost to costly sources, and multi-fidelity methods do not state how many costly evaluations an imported ordering of the candidates replaces. We test whether that ordering, with its margins, reduces the evaluations needed to reach a given ranking quality, and whether the saving can be measured for each route. TENKi (Transfer-ensemble Knowledge Inheritance) records ranking agreement against budget while a ranking model is fitted to queries that order several candidates at once, with the donor ordering entered as a prior whose trust is learned from incoming results. The evidence is 261,053 archived band-gap records from eight sources, 171 semiconductors with gaps computed on demand, and an aluminium–magnesium–silicon (Al–Mg–Si) alloy pool computed with DFT and molecular dynamics. Queries ranking four candidates outperform pairwise comparisons on every source, a donor prior replaces nearly half of the early measurement budget, and a trained query-selection policy reaches the ranking quality of random selection with fewer evaluations on held-out sources, whereas hand-written rules do not. An ordering from the generalised gradient approximation cuts hybrid-functional compute about sixfold, while an archived ordering that lacks the alloys gives no saving at fixed trust; for Al–Mg–Si, a foundation-potential ordering lowers the DFT compute needed to find eight of the ten most stable compounds from 19% to 5%. The saving depends on direction and coverage, and the agreement-versus-budget curve separates disagreement that further sampling removes from gaps that remain, so a campaign can use these curves to decide which source to compute first, how far to trust it, and when further evaluations stop improving the ranking.

item.title: Graded revision lets autonomous campaigns update symbolic laws of SiGeC semiconductors from mixed-fidelity evidence
item.description: Autonomous materials campaigns combine published measurements, simulations at several levels of theory and curated compilations whose errors are known in kind but not in size. A value off the current law may be an error, a measurement under a special condition, or a lead to missing physics, and an outlier filter discards all three alike. Machine unlearning removes data from neural networks by costly or approximate retraining, and provenance records locate data origins without identifying which conclusions to revise. We tested whether nine graded revision actions on sourcetagged evidence, from labelling or reweighting rows to forgetting them, confine each correction to conclusions named in advance. The actions operate on symbolic laws fitted by HG-SR, a symbolic-regression engine whose terms record their supporting evidence, and were applied to the lattice thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex and SiGeC, which limits heat removal from SiGe transistors. The pipeline corrected an undesigned unit error, caught mislabelled and amorphous simulation rows from their structure, split the literature by microstructure and issued a conductivity law with a declared validity domain. Of twelve decisions on flagged values, four found errors; the other eight kept the value, five as special conditions (microstructure, another alloy, melting, box size, nonlinear response) and three as leads to physics the law lacked. For SiGeC it showed that carbon leaves the lattice as SiC and named in advance the one weak input of the germanium-saving claim; pre-registered tests of that input changed only the named conclusions for a leg operated from 300 to 1100 K, leaving its composition and carbon content unchanged. Because the SiC scattering contrast fell with particle radius roughly as R−4, 2.5 nm SiC replaces 14–16% of the germanium at equal lattice thermal conductivity (8–9% at 5 nm). Corrections become targeted errata, not rebuilds, and less germanium eases demand for a by-product metal of constrained supply.

item.title: Evaluating transfer across modalities in autonomous materials systems
item.description: A power device needs a wide-gap semiconductor and a heat-treated Al–Mg–Si alloy to cool it, and both draw on sources that disagree: band gaps from several levels of density functional theory (DFT) and from measurement, alloy formation energies from DFT and interatomic potentials. Multi-fidelity methods combine such sources only through paired values on a common scale and do not state in advance whether one source’s guidance holds in another. We test whether the relative differences between candidates, which lead and by how much, are preserved across sources whose values disagree. PEGKi infers relative ratings of decision bodies (any rule that ranks candidates) from comparison outcomes within each source, and scores every donor-to-receiver route with a robustness certificate or a refusal. The evidence is 261,053 archived band-gap records from eight sources and an Al–Mg–Si pool where every query runs a DFT or molecular-dynamics calculation. Orderings alone recover the accuracy ladder of the DFT levels, and experiment spreads material classes about twice as widely as the generalised gradient approximation. Transfer follows the database of origin more than the functional, and routing learned from measured campaigns outperforms the fixed default at every query size. For the alloy, the score picks each potential’s room-temperature run as donor at heat-treatment temperatures, the best measured choice in five of six cases, and discounts the two potentials that predict Mg2Si to be unstable. Relative margins therefore transfer where values do not, so a campaign can rate whose knowledge to reuse before committing compute or instrument time.

item.title: Processing history attached to each value separates conflicting evidence on metastable (Si)GeSn semiconductors
item.description: GeSn and SiGeSn with several per cent Sn are metastable direct-gap group-IV semiconductors: anneals, contact sinters or hot measurements can move Sn out of the lattice, so a value describes the film at one point in its processing, not its composition alone. Published values rarely carry that history, and machine-learned simulations add values whose errors are known in kind but not in size; two disagreeing values may reflect an error or two different samples. The hypothesis tested was that recording the processing history with every value separates conflicting evidence that composition and temperature leave unresolved. Each value was stored as one event of a time-resolved evidence hypergraph, whose entries link states before and after, defect species, process step, source and time window on separate clocks for sample processing and campaign decisions; defect reactions must balance. The record held 551 literature values from 163 anneal series, 3028 defect events from molecular dynamics with the machine-learned potential MACE-MP-0, and 159 campaign entries. MACE-MP-0 kept Ge0.88Sn0.12 crystalline for 0.5 ns only at 500 K; at 600 and 700 K the model lattice disordered, so a 0.13 eV hop activation energy across 500 to 700 K measures disorder, not a barrier. The same potential bound Sn to a vacancy by 0.43± 0.08 eV. Literature activation energies for Sn diffusion in Ge-rich material spanned 1.13 to 3.10 eV but fell into groups no wider than 0.7 eV once anneal regime and starting state were recorded, and an oxide cap alone decided whether a Si0.08Ge0.88Sn0.04 film degraded at 550 °C. These conflicts follow processing history rather than composition, and a foundation potential’s dynamics hold only within a stated temperature range. Anneals of metastable films between 380 and 650 °C therefore call for the low-temperature film activation energy, not the implanted-bulk value.

item.title: Provenance records predict which multi-scale conclusions a foundation-potential release can change in SiGeC semiconductors
item.description: Multi-scale simulations of semiconductor alloys rest on foundation interatomic potentials (machine-learned force models trained on large density-functional databases), re-released as training data grow. A release changes defect energies and phonon stiffness and, through them, the recipes and design verdicts downstream; recomputing everything is costly, and recomputing nothing leaves conclusions that may no longer hold. Workflow records list every result downstream of a calculation, not which could change a decision. We tested whether the conclusions a release can change are predictable from a campaign’s provenance record (a record of which calculation fed which result) before any rerun and settled by recomputing only the predicted units. The chain served a SiGeC design question (germanium content, carbon content and SiC particle size for low lattice thermal conductivity), with MACE-MP-0 replaced by MACE-MPA-0 and all predictions and decision rules fixed in advance. From the record, 49 of 128 record entries were reached, 24 conclusions were classified by their margin to a decision threshold, and four recompute units were named. Recomputing those units (70 relaxations, 91 molecular-dynamics runs) settled 20 conclusions: none changed outside the predicted set (exact 95% upper bound on the miss rate 0.24), eight of nine flagged as at risk held, and one, Ge attraction to the first shell around a SiC particle, reversed by less than a millielectronvolt past its threshold, while the conclusion it served (no germanium-depleted zone forms) held. Magnitudes moved more than assumed: the energy carbon gains by precipitating as SiC grew by 0.65–0.75 eV against an assumed 0.3 eV; the recipe and the germanium saving held. Recomputation cost 3.5 CPU-task-hours and 354 GPU-hours, 2.2 times the GPU estimate scaled from the recorded runs. Decisions whose margins exceed a measured release shift can be carried across a release with a recorded check; magnitudes need recomputation, and explicit records of each result’s inputs and code would make the prediction a lookup.

item.title: Covering and loss-tolerant batch designs guarantee what autonomous campaigns sample in SiGeC semiconductors
item.description: Self-driving laboratories plan experiments in batches and lose runs to cracked pellets, tripped furnaces and cancelled compute jobs. Their planners give no guarantee about which combinations of processing variables a batch has sampled, so an interaction between two variables can go unnoticed. The hypothesis tested was that covering designs from software testing supply that guarantee at a run cost known in advance. A covering batch samples every pair of variable levels at least once, or twice so any single lost run leaves the guarantee intact; greedy follow-up batches touched every uncertain region with few runs; and eight evidence sources were assigned to composition and temperature regimes at least cost. In a pre-registered study of heat transport in the boron-or phosphorus-doped nanostructured SiGeC semiconductor (six coupled variables, 9000 combinations), a covering batch sampled every two-factor combination with 33 runs, the doubled batch kept that property under any single loss, and one-factor-at-a-time screening, which never varies two factors together, picked a recipe 33% above the best (22% under the SiC contrast measured later). On 16 molecular dynamics recipes the planner never saw, covering kept its guarantee but predicted no better than random batches, because only Ge content and temperature moved the response there. A covering-designed molecular dynamics campaign on strained SiGe device films found heat flow across a film grown on Si 12 to 18% above relaxed bulk, with heat flow along it unchanged. Covering is valuable while the relevance of each factor is unknown: an autonomous campaign can state, before its first run, which combinations its conclusions speak to.

item.title: Hash-committed pre-registration and exact unlearning make belief revisions in autonomous SiGeC semiconductor campaigns checkable
item.description: Autonomousmaterials laboratories revise conclusions fromevidence sources (calculations,machine-learned potentials, databases, furnace runs) whose errors are known in kind but not in size. These revisions are self-reported, so a reader cannot check that no batch was dropped or that a retraction removed what it claims; verifiable unlearning covers only erasure from trained machinelearning models. The aim is a record that lets anyone check every revision without trusting the campaign. Full checkability is hypothesised to be affordable when beliefs are compact symbolic models, whose clean retrain takes seconds. Designs are hashed onto an append-only campaign record before runs start, raw outputs are committed before analysis, and revisions are verified by deterministic re-execution. Four pre-registered campaigns on heat transport in SiGe and SiGeC semiconductors (molecular dynamics, machine-learned relaxations, phonon transport, an experimental database) test the scheme. The record keeps failed checks, refuted predictions and set-aside evidence in view, and an independent verifier re-checks it in about three seconds. It meets pharmaceutical data-integrity rules; separating a measurement’s influence on fitted laws from the measurement reconciles the European right to erasure with mandatory retention. Materials claims, such as howmuch germanium carbon can replace, can thus be adopted and extended on an inspectable record.

item.title: How the fruit fly connectome can help autonomous materials discovery
item.description: Autonomous laboratories for two-dimensional semiconductors pair a recipe planner with instruments that return in situ spectra every few seconds. Some decisions are too fast for the planner: stop a failing selenization anneal, flag a flake that is not the logged material, or end an ion irradiation at a set vacancy density, from a few examples, on a small computer at the instrument. The fruit fly takes decisions of this form with two structures whose wiring is measured at synapse level: the mushroom body, a one-shot memory for odours, and the ventral nerve cord, which turns a few descending commands into local reflexes. We asked which instrument jobs models wired from these connectomes do better than engineered tools. A mushroom-body model of 685 projection neurons and 5,177 Kenyon cells read one Raman band per glomerulus; over 20 paired seeds, on simulated selenization Raman streams and on Ar+ irradiation anchored in published in situ spectra, it lost the fewest flakes when one failed run taught a stop rule (3.3 of 30, against 3.9 for a nearest neighbour), read vacancy density from its sparse code with less error than from the raw spectrum (5.5 % against 6.4 %), and ran in 0.30 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5 within 152 kB. A stop decided at the furnace, as the nerve cord decides reflexes, prevented the losses of a planner that needed 60 s per turn (0.15 against 10.7 flakes of 30). It did not choose recipes. In three animals and after training, measured wiring matched a degree-preserving shuffle, and the nerve-cord wiring matched a ridge regression: the connectome contributes an architecture and wiring statistics, not a partner map. As hardware, the fixed wiring can be binary and each plastic synapse needs about 64 levels. The connectome supplies a low-cost reflex layer under the planner, not a replacement.

item.title: Compound-specific memory demand determines when a research group and a computing centre benefit from sharing information in two-dimensional semiconductor screening
item.description: Screening two-dimensional semiconductors with density functional theory (DFT), the standard electronic-structure method, involves two parties who know each other only qualitatively: a research group holding the candidate list and a computing centre that knows its nodes. Sharing information helps either party only if a calculation’s demand on the node depends on the compound. Thirty transition-metal dichalcogenide layers (MX2; M = Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W; X = S, Se, Te) in 1T and 2H structures were screened with Quantum ESPRESSO at the PBE level, recording each calculation’s duration and memory, then supercells up to 3328 electrons and preregistered paired comparisons of no sharing against a job-placing broker. Nine layers have PBE gaps in the 1.0–2.0 eV window of transistor channels and photodetectors, seven after spin–orbit coupling; single-layer 2H cells keep the same nine, and chalcogen-vacancy hop barriers follow the gap, also in Janus layers. In primitive cells and 3×3 supercells, demand followed calculation stage and cell size, which the centre already knows, and no arrangement raised throughput. At 8×8 supercells, compounds of equal electron count differed in memory by 23–32% near node capacity; one disclosed memory-class bit per job raised the centre’s throughput 1.133-fold under memory-reservation charging, but not on single-layer pools, whose memory classes nearly coincide. The group gained no resolvable advantage and job timings revealed the compound, so the hypothesis that the broker benefits both parties was rejected. A gap screen needs batching rather than disclosure; defect and heterostructure supercells justify disclosing one memory class per job.

item.title: Simple Modification to Minimize Ionomer Poisoning in Carbodiimide Synthesized Pt-Rare Earth Catalysts
item.description: Platinum rare earth (Pt-RE) alloys show promise as oxygen reduction reaction catalysts due to their improved activity and durability over conventional Pt-based catalysts. However, their synthesis has remained relatively complicated due to REs high affinity for oxygen. Recently, carbodiimide-mediated synthesis has shown promise under relatively moderate conditions, although it results in nanoparticle formation mostly on the carbon support exterior. We introduce a simple “wet-mix” modification that allows metallic precursors to diffuse into the pores of the Ketjenblack support as nucleation sites, affording a larger proportion of nanoparticles inside of the pores of the carbon black. XRD, HR-TEM, XPS and XAS, indicate higher Pt2Gd formation for the conventional carbodiimide route; our synthesis produces Pt2Gd with a small fraction of polycrystalline PtGd. Rotating-disk electrode studies showed that a high ionomer loading does not depress the mass activity, specific activity, or ECSA of the wet-synthesized catalyst. We validate this work in 12 cm2 single-cell PEMFC studies under H2/O2, with specific activity improvement of 2.27×, and mass activity improvement of 3.04×. While the durability of the catalyst has not significantly improved, we propose reduced ionomer poisoning of the Pt2Gd catalyst resulting from our simple “wet-mix” modification to the carbodiimide route improves ORR activity.

item.title: An artificial macrophage reveals the impact of nitric oxide microenvironments on bacterial viability
item.description: Nitric oxide (NO) emitted from immune cells such as macrophages plays an important role in combating bacterial pathogens. Yet studying ephemeral NO-mediated interactions in real time, quantitatively, and at the single-cell level has been technically challenging. Here we present an “artificial macrophage”: a live-cell imaging platform that overcomes these challenges by leveraging electrochemistry to generate micropatterned NO gradients at infection-relevant concentrations. We achieve this capability using a biocompatible electrocatalyst that selectively transforms ammonia into NO in biological media. Using Pseudomonas aeruginosa as a model NO-responsive pathogen, we show that the NO microenvironment, influenced by both extracellular NO concentrations and NO gradients experienced by cells, underpins NO’s bactericidal efficacy for individual surface-associated cells. Our results highlight that considering NO’s reaction-diffusion, rather than just its local concentration, is key to understanding how the extracellular microenvironment affects single-cell bacterial viability. Spatiotemporal control of NO microenvironments using our live-cell imaging platform will advance studies of diverse cell types that regularly encounter NO.

item.title: Are Molecular Foundation Models Ready for Free Energy Simulations?
item.description: Foundation models for atomistic simulations offer broadly applicable potentialenergy surfaces that can either be applied in a zero-shot manner (without domainspecific retraining) or fine-tuned to the task at hand. Their accuracy is typically judged by energy and force errors on near-equilibrium data, yet it remains largely unclear whether these metrics translate into reliable free-energy landscapes. Here, enhanced sampling can be a particularly demanding test: simulations are driven far from equilibrium into sparsely trained regions and held there over long trajectories, so that small systematic errors in forces or relative energies can accumulate and distort predicted populations, transition pathways, and barriers. We assess several molecular foundation models trained on different dataset sizes and architectures (including models with explicit long-range electrostatics) in prototypical metadynamics and umbrella sampling simulations. Our results show that recent foundation models can reproduce simple gas-phase free-energy profiles with near-reference accuracy, while more complex multidimensional and solvated free-energy landscapes remain challenging. However, assessing their performance in these systems is further complicated by limitations in current sampling protocols and the lack of well-defined reference data. These findings highlight the need for more rigorous sampling protocols and reliable benchmarks to systematically assess the accuracy of future molecular foundation models in free-energy calculations.

item.title: Polymethylsilsesquioxane Aerogel-like Xerogels via a Surfactant-Free Base-Catalyzed Process
item.description: Highly insulating polymethylsilsesquioxane (PMSQ) aerogel-like xerogels were prepared from methyltrimethoxysilane in 2-propanol (IPA)/water using 10 wt % aqueous tetraethylammonium hydroxide in a one-step reaction without an acid step or surfactant. Fine interconnected skeletons were obtained after ambient-pressure drying. Infrared spectroscopy and solid-state 29Si nuclear magnetic resonance indicated fewer residual silanols in the dried material than in a two-step reference. A 20-fold scale-up gave effective thermal conductivities of 0.018 W m−1 K−1 for granular material and 0.021 W m−1 K−1 for a PMSQ-filled panel with a polycarbonate casing at 20 °C. This provides a simple route to insulating granular PMSQ.

item.title: Information Dynamics Explains Chemical Reactions: A Unified Framework from NaI Photodissociation to H2 Formation
item.description: Chemical reactions are fundamentally the motion of atomic nuclei on potential energy surfaces. However, there is a methodological gap between quantum chemistry calculations and dynamical simulations: constructing potential energy surfaces is complicated, non-adiabatic couplings are difficult to treat, and different reaction types lack a unified language. In this work we introduce the information dynamics framework, reformulating chemical reactions as a three-element system: virtual space (potential energy surface rules), real space (initial wave packet data), and coupling matrix (projection mechanism). The virtual space defines the absolutely allowed region for nuclear motion, the real space provides the observed distribution of initial positions and momenta, and the coupling matrix drives the system toward a steady-state product according to the virtual space topology (gradient flow for a single surface or Landau-Zener transitions for two crossing surfaces). We validate the framework with three classic reactions: (1) NaI photodissociation (nonadiabatic, two crossing surfaces)—simulated dissociation yield 65.3% ± 1.5%, matching Zewail’s femtochemistry experiment (65%); (2) Cl2 photodissociation (adiabatic, single repulsive surface)dissociation yield 100%, mean relative kinetic energy 3.84 eV, in agreement with literature values;

item.title: Ligand Protonation Tunes Hydride-Transfer Thermochemistry in an Iron Metal-Ligand Cooperative Catalyst
item.description: Cyclopentadienone iron complexes are established metal-ligand cooperative hydrogenation catalysts, yet their bifunctional reactivity complicates the independent evaluation of proton- and hydride-transfer thermodynamics. Here, room-temperature H2-splitting enables deconvolution of these contributions, affording a new anionic hydride with a hydricity of 39.0 kcal·mol-1. Ligand protonation weakens hydride-donor strength by 10 kcal mol-1, highlighting protonation-state control of reactivity in MLC catalysis.

item.title: Optical Design of Low-Haze Transparent Wood
item.description: Transparent wood (TW) composite is a structural optical material for light‑transmitting applications. TW with low haze (scattering) remains challenging due to multiple light‑scattering mechanisms at different length scales. Interfacial debonding, limited polymer accessibility in the cell wall, and refractive index (RI) mismatch between wood and polymer phases contribute to forward scattering and haze. Here we establish an optical design strategy to reduce haze/scattering in TW composites by suppressing scattering sources. Chemical modification through NaOH swelling and acetylation is employed to reduce optical defects, while the polymer phase is tailored by tuning the RI. A series of TW composites enables decoupling of different scattering mechanisms and analysis of their contributions through transmittance, haze, angular light‑distribution, and ultra-fast time resolved measurements. RI tuning combined with chemical reduction of interfacial optical defects leads to a strong decrease in haze (down to ~ 45% for a 1mm thick sample). A more isotropic transmitted light distribution confirms suppression of refraction-based scattering. The study provides a mechanism-based framework for designing low-haze TW and other cellulose-based optical composites.

item.title: Site-Selective Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics and Its Integration with Replica-Exchange Methods
item.description: We developed site-selective Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (ssGaMD), which selectively enhances molecular motions associated with a specified region or set of interactions. The method allows selected dihedral, electrostatic, and Lennard–Jones energy terms to be biased independently or in combination, while limiting direct biasing of the rest of the system. ssGaMD can be combined with replica-exchange umbrella sampling (ssGaREUS) or temperature replicaexchange molecular dynamics (ssGaREMD) to further enhance the sampling of association and dissociation processes and conformational changes. We implemented these methods in the GENESIS MD simulation software and applied them to aspirin binding to β-cyclodextrin, PP1 binding to Src kinase, and Trp-cage folding. Selectively boosting interactions involved in binding efficiently promoted molecular association and dissociation, while combining ssGaMD with replica-exchange methods accelerated the convergence of binding and folding free-energy landscapes. These methods offer a flexible approach to studying ligand binding and other biomolecular processes in which slow dynamics are governed by specific local interactions.

item.title: Looking Beyond KD for Aptamer Validation: Disentangling Specific Aptamer Binding from Electrostatic Association for Basic Protein Targets
item.description: Nucleic acid aptamers provide a simple, cost-effective alternative to antibodies for targeting biomolecular analytes from ions to large protein complexes. However, the interactions of these nucleic-acid based structures in vivo remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we report the seemingly pervasive electrostatic association between nucleic acids and high isoelectric point proteins under biological conditions. Such non-specific binding runs the risk of convoluting aptamer selection and validation, while also potentially interfering with nucleic acid-based nanotechnologies in vivo. Through our explorations, we identify several methods to disentangle sequence-specific aptamer interactions from non-specific electrostatic association, allowing for discrimination between binding modes. We also identify dissociation rate (koff) and equilibrium binding response (Req) as potentially better discriminators than KD for isolating and validating true sequence-specific aptamers.

item.title: Mild acid promoted bromination with H2O2/NaBr at room temperature inspired by flavin-dependent halogenase (FDH)
item.description: Bromination is an important and frequently used organic transformation. Many elegant and reliable bromination methods have been well established; however, limitations still exist, thus calling for more sustainable approaches with broader substrate scope, better selectivity, milder condition and lower cost. In this manuscript, an effective bromination method has been established utilizing low-toxic and cost-friendly carboxylic acid/NaBr/H2O2, including bromination of (hetero)arenes, decarboxylative bromination of (hetero)aryl/vinyl carboxylic acid, ipsohydroxylation-bromination of (hetero)aryl boronic acids/esters, hydroxybromination of alkyne/alkene, and 𝛼-bromination of ketone. Broad substrate scope, good functional group tolerance, operation-friendly procedure, moderate to excellent yields, and late-stage bromination of small molecule natural products and drugs have been achieved. The carboxylic acid was hypothesized to play dual roles as providing H-bond, proton donor and acceptor in this reaction. Compared many previously reported bromination methods, this method shows evidently better sustainability, and can serve as a useful synthetic tool for related research.

item.title: The Regularized Frozen Natural Orbital approach to CASPT2: extension to Restricted Active Space wave functions, different multiplicities and assessment of correlation effects
item.description: The frozen natural orbital (FNO) method is a well-known approximation that significantly reduces the cost of many-body perturbation theory treatments for obtaining correlation energies in a systematic and controlled manner, enabling the simulation of larger and more realistic molecular systems. Here, we implement FNO on top of restricted active-space self-consistent field (RASSCF) wave function within second-order perturbation theory, leading to the FNO-RASPT2 method. To account for the additional approximations incurred when using restricted RASSCF wave functions, as well as to apply it to states of different molecular charge and spin multiplicity, we introduce a regularisation approach via a level-shift in the orbital deletion procedure, which helps avoid singularities resulting from vanishing denominators due to the reduced occupation of restricted (active) virtual orbitals and that we show does not significantly influence the final energies obtained. Numerical results on vertical excitation energies showcase the FNO to be up to ∼3.5 faster than the parent computation while retaining ∼95% of the dynamic correlation energy and being within 0.1 eV of the reference calculation, with the CASPT2 equations-the main bottleneck in large molecular systems-registering over an order of magnitude speed-up. An in-depth analysis shows the regularized FNO approach to retain electron correlation appropriately for internal and semi-internal contributions, while displaying larger deviations for the external term, which originates from the initial FNO truncation based on an approximated one-electron reduced density matrix. Ongoing efforts are directed towards improving and extending our current implementation to the calculation of analytic gradients and non-adiabatic couplings to enable faster non-adiabatic molecular dynamics simulations in larger and more realistic molecular systems.

item.title: Describing the Fluxional Dynamics of Sub-nanoscale Clusters with Markov State Modeling
item.description: Fluxionality, or the population of and interconversion between multiple structures, has long been suggested to be relevant for understanding the physical and catalytic behavior of sub-nanoscale metal clusters on an oxide support. Much of this treatment has, however, been thermodynamic, neglecting direct exploration of the timescales for interconversion between di!erent isomers. Previously, we exploited machine-learned interatomic potentials, combined with automatic process exploration (MLIP-APE) to identify isomerization networks for MgO-supported Pd clusters, capturing all barriers for cluster restructuring. In the current work, we demonstrate a new analysis approach based on Markov State Modeling (MSM) which captures the complex contribution of multiple timescales on the overall fluxional dynamic behavior over a range of cluster sizes. This overall fluxional behavior can then be classified between the extremes of highly dynamic “labile” clusters, to “rigid” clusters which exhibit much less dynamic behavior. These dynamics are of particular interest when using fluxional clusters for catalysis, as these dynamics could influence the observed catalytic reactions. Ultimately, this work demonstrates a rigorous and general approach to investigate the dynamics of reaction networks of well-defined states.

item.title: Thioethers as alkyl donors in electrochemical C–O and C–N bond forming reactions
item.description: A catalyst- and fluoride-free electrochemical method for the use of readily available thioethers as alkyl donors in C-O and C-N bond formation to furnish ethers, esters, and N-alkylated products is reported. The protocol exhibits broad functional group tolerance and is compatible with structurally complex substrates. Cyclic voltammetry studies rationalize the distinct behaviour of oxygen and nitrogen nucleophiles and guide the optimization of the electrochemical conditions, enabling the formation of coupled products from starting materials with both matched and mismatched redox potentials.

item.title: Cold Plasma Induced 3D Printing of Hydrogels
item.description: Control over when and where gelation occurs is central to the fabrication of structured soft materials, yet most approaches rely on chemical additives or uniform bulk triggers. Here, we show that cold plasma provides an external, reagent-free route to spatial and temporal control over gelation in low molecular weight hydrogel systems. Plasma exposure induces a localised decrease in pH at the plasma–liquid interface, triggering self-assembly and gel formation only in the treated region. This external plasma-induced self-assembly method enables direct writing of gel features from precursor solutions without embedded triggers, construction of three-dimensional architectures, and control over local mechanical properties through plasma dose. Our approach also allows simultaneous formation of metal nanoparticles within gels, yielding spatially confined composite and catalytic soft materials.

item.title: Nanoscale Phase Engineering and Magnetic Property Enhancement in High-Entropy Alloy Nanoparticles by Continuous Microparticle Laser Fragmentation in Liquid
item.description: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs) offer compositional and structural tunability for applications, like water splitting, H2O2 production, or magnetocaloric technologies. Therefore, the interplay between composition, structure, and functionality is of significant interest for materials´ functionality optimization. Microparticle laser fragmentation in liquid flow (MP-LFL) is an emerging scalable method for nanoalloy production, but remains underexplored for HEA NPs. Here, we investigate CrFeCoNiX (X = Ga, Cu, Mo) HEA NPs fabricated by MP-LFL in ethanol and examine how compositional variations affect elemental homogeneity, size, phase structure, and magnetic properties. Microscopy, diffraction, size analysis, and magnetometry reveal particle sizes of 6-7 nm and pronounced differences in phase structures, ranging from single-phase fcc and biphasic fcc/bcc to amorphous structures, partially contrasting the initial feedstock microparticle structures. The low saturation magnetization (Ms, 310 K) of the as-synthesized superparamagnetic NPs increases strongly after in situ annealing by approximately 4-, 3-, or 24-fold for Ga-, Cu-, and Mo-containing NPs, respectively, coinciding with structural and elemental rearrangements. In contrast, the feedstock microparticles show no comparable increase, highlighting the role of the initial phase constitution in determining magnetic properties. Moreover, MP-LFL enables production of ~0.4 g h-1, with a record picosecond MP-LFL mass yield of ~60%, leaving room for further optimization and high throughput.

item.title: Ring Opening of Oxiranes with Amines Using Iodolium Salts as XB-Precatalysts
item.description: Herein, we report the nucleophilic ring-opening of oxiranes with substituted amines using N-heterocycle-substituted iodolium salts (NHISs) as Lewis acid pre-catalysts. Using the ring-opening of styrene oxide by aniline as a model reaction, we demonstrate that NHISs enable efficient β-aminoalcohol formation at room temperature and with pre-catalyst loadings as low as 2.5 mol%. The optimized protocol was successfully applied to a broad range of substituted oxiranes and amines, affording the corresponding β-aminoalcohols in isolated yields of up to 98%. Based on control experiments and recent literature examples, we show that the iodolium salt is not a simple spectator but, under the reaction conditions, undergoes an amine-induced intramolecular aryl–aryl coupling to generate an electron-deficient iodoarene and an ammonium borate salt in situ. On this basis, we propose a dual activation mechanism in which halogen-bond (XB) donor activation of the epoxide operates in concert with an in situ generated β-hydroxyammonium co-catalyst.

item.title: Molybdenum and Tungsten Dinitrogen Complexes Supported by Modified pentaPod Ligands: Implications on the Activation of N2 and its Conversion to NH3
item.description: The pentaPod (pentadentate tetrapodal phosphine) ligand P5R with PMe2 or phospholane (Pln) donors offers the opportunity to investigate how small changes in the ligand framework affect the properties of the corresponding transition-metal complexes. Here, we examine the influence of replacing the propyl with ethyl groups in the trident part of the pentaPod ligand with regard to N2 activation as well as N2-to-NH3 conversion by the corresponding Mo(0)N2 and W(0)N2 complexes. A comparison of the DFT-optimized structures of the original P5R and the shortened etP5R pentaPod complexes reveals important structural differences that influence N2 activation. The geometric and electronic structure results obtained from DFT are checked by comprehensive spectroscopic and electrochemical studies of the new etP5R-supported molybdenum and tungsten systems as well as through an investigation of their ability to (catalytically) generate NH3.

item.title: Central Atom Driven Modulation of Electron Transfer in Alkyne-Protected Ag14 Nanoclusters
item.description: Single-atom doping at the cluster core is an effective strategy for modulating the molecule-like properties of monolayer-protected nanoclusters. In this study, we systematically synthesized a pair of alkyne-protected silver nanoclusters, in which the central template anion of one nanocluster was replaced by a copper atom in the other. Incorporation of copper significantly quenched the photoluminescence of the nanocluster while enhancing its electron-transfer capability through modification of the electronic structure. Theoretical calculations further revealed that the central copper atom contributes directly to the frontier molecular orbitals. This work represents an important step toward the development of atomically precise nanochemistry, demonstrating how precise structural tailoring of alkyne-protected silver nanoclusters can be used to regulate their functional properties.

item.title: How to tame your bromine: bandgap tuning of solvent-free hybrid perovskites in a vapor transport deposition process
item.description: We present a sequential physical vapor and gas phase transport deposition process for batchcapable formation of metal halide perovskite films, applicable to single- and multi-junction solar cells. After evaporating porous Cs-containing Pb halides via physical vapor deposition onto the substrate or bottom cell, we use a quartz furnace to deposit the organic precursor, formamidinium iodide (FAI), onto this inorganic scaffold via vapor transport deposition. Ammonia is used as carrier gas to prevent decomposition of FAI. The resulting perovskite is already present in the photoactive alpha phase. The process time can be minimized down to 15 min, depending on the scaffold, as no subsequent annealing is required. Notably all contacting layers in this work, including self-assembled molecules and passivation, are also fabricated with solvent-free processes. We note an occurring halide exchange reaction between the FAI in vapor phase and Br in the scaffold and present a proposed reaction scheme. By utilizing this reaction, we can vary the resulting bandgap of the perovskite to fit to the requirements for tandem applications, showing a broad process window. The resulting champion cell (1.66 eV) created with this approach reaches 18.3% power conversion efficiency, with a photoluminescence quantum yield of 1.6 % on full cell stacks.

item.title: Compartmentalized Microgels with Programmed Acoustic Anisotropy for Orthogonal Ultrasound-Triggered Motion and Cargo Release
item.description: Compartmentalization is a fundamental organizational principle in nature, enabling anisotropy required for controlled locomotion and spatiotemporal regulation of biological processes. Inspired by this principle, we present a one-step strategy to fabricate compartmentalized anisotropic microgels via liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) in aqueous droplets. Upon sodium chloride addition, concentrated N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAAm) solutions spontaneously separate into NIPAAm-rich and NIPAAm-poor phases. Integrating this process into microfluidic droplets followed by photopolymerization enables continuous fabrication of anisotropic PNIPAAm microgels with two compartments of distinct stiffness. Synthetic and biological macromolecules can be selectively loaded into different compartments according to their polarity. Crucially, LLPS-generated acoustic contrast enables two independently addressable functionalities under biocompatible ultrasound (US). Lowfrequency, low-intensity US induces propulsion at speeds of approximately 10 microgel diameters per second without cargo release, whereas high-frequency, higher-intensity US at biocompatible settings selectively degrades one compartment, enabling on-demand cargo release. Complementary computer simulations further elucidate the physical mechanisms underlying acoustically driven motion. This work establishes LLPS-driven compartmentalization as a design principle for multifunctional colloidal microrobots with independently programmable propulsion and cargo release, opening new avenues for targeted drug delivery and soft robotics.

item.title: Genome Mining-Guided Discovery of Polyketide-Tropolone Hybrids Reveals Their Biosynthetic Logic and Antitumor Activity
item.description: 2 ABSTRACT: Tropolone-containing natural products display diverse biological activities, yet characterized fungal tropolone hybrids are dominated by sesquiterpene-derived systems, leaving polyketide-tropolone hybridization largely unexplored. Here, genome mining guided by conserved tropolone biosynthetic enzymes and an unusual dual-polyketide synthase architecture led to the discovery of fusariolones A–E and semifusariolone A from Fusarium sp. WA57, defining a distinct family of fungal polyketide-tropolone hybrids. Heterologous pathway reconstitution supported fusABCDEF as the minimal gene set for scaffold assembly and revealed a biosynthetic logic in which a canonical tropolone pathway converges with a highly reducing polyketide synthase. The resulting linear pentaene hydrocarbon represents, to the best of our knowledge, the first such intermediate identified in fungal natural product biosynthesis and supports a proposed FusF-mediated dehydration/hetero-Diels-Alder cascade in scaffold construction. Fusariolone A displayed low-nanomolar antiproliferative activity with pronounced selectivity toward K562 and HT-29 cells. In HT-29 cells, it suppressed DNA synthesis, altered cell cycle progression, and increased apoptosis, while also reducing xenograftassociated fluorescence in zebrafish. Together, these findings establish a distinct biosynthetic strategy for polyketide-tropolone hybrid assembly and expand the chemical and functional space of fungal tropolone natural products.

item.title: In Situ Mapping of Aqueous CO2 during the Electrochemical CO2 Reduction Reaction
item.description: Electrochemical interfaces feature dynamically evolving local reactant distributions that strongly influence catalytic behavior. In electrochemical CO2 reduction (CO2RR), the low solubility and limited diffusion of CO2 generate highly non-uniform local reaction environments near electrochemical interfaces. However, the actual spatial distribution of dissolved CO2 within the interfacial structure under operating conditions remains poorly understood due to limited experimental visualization methods that probe interfacial structure. Here, we introduce an in situ ratiometric fluorescent labeling strategy with a CO2-sensitive chemosensor to directly visualize dissolved CO2 distributions during CO2RR. Using a pyrene-modified fluorescent chemosensor, we directly visualize the spatial distribution and dynamic evolution of local dissolved CO2 concentrations near electrochemical interfaces. The measurements reveal pronounced spatial heterogeneity in the CO2RR microenvironment, dynamic evolution of gas-liquid-solid interfaces, and unexpectedly strong local CO2 enrichment. Dissolved CO2 concentrations near the interface approached ~84.4 ± 27.5 mM. Beyond CO2RR, this work establishes fluorescent labeling as a general operando visualization strategy for probing local reactant distributions and interfacial mass transport processes in electrochemical systems.

item.title: Accelerating the deployment of nitrogen diversion and recovery technologies in water resource recovery facilities
item.description: Nitrogen recovery from human excreta is advancing rapidly at the laboratory scale, yet its potential in full-scale water resource recovery facilities (WRRFs) remains unrealized. To expedite the deployment of nitrogen recovery technology across diverse WRRF configurations, an agile and standardized framework is needed to predict plant-wide operational impacts and prioritize deployment pathways. Here, we developed and applied an open-source benchmarking framework comprising 18 representative WRRF configurations to evaluate three early-stage nitrogen recovery upgrades – upstream urine diversion (UD), mainstream hydrogel adsorption (HA), and sidestream electrochemical stripping (ECS). WRRFs’ operational performance is configuration-dependent: biological nutrient removal configurations, particularly the Johannesburg process and modified Bardenpho membrane bioreactor with anaerobic digestion, exhibit the largest operating expenditure savings for WRRFs across all three upgrades. Approaches that recover >40% of total nitrogen (UD covering 100% served population, or 100% UD, and HA) from the influent can reduce OPEX by 31% to 56%, whereas lower recovery (10% UD and ECS) still reduce OPEX by 10% to 15%. Together, these results identify promising deployment pathways for early-stage nitrogen recovery technologies and provide a scalable approach for evaluating other resource recovery upgrades.

item.title: RetroMol: Knowledge Distillation of Energy-Based Retrosynthesis Models
item.description: Retrosynthesis prediction is a central task in computer-aided synthesis planning, and synthesizability remains a persistent bottleneck in AI-driven molecular and materials discovery. We introduce RetroMol, a family of compact text-based models that transfers an energy-based critic’s ranking of candidate reactant sets into the generator itself. RetroBase, an 11M-parameter transformer encoderdecoder trained on two-reactant USPTO reactions, achieves Top-1 and Top-5 accuracies of 46.8% and 67.8% on a held-out test split. RetroERM, an energybased model over molecular fingerprint counts, scores RetroBase’s candidates, and its ranking preferences are distilled back into the generator. The distilled model, RetroDistil, reaches 52.6% Top-1 and 73.5% Top-5 under identical data and evaluation, improving on RetroBase by 5.7–6.8 points at Top-1/3/5 with no reranking stage at inference and no increase in model size. Distilling a critic is therefore a practical way to improve a compact retrosynthesis generator without larger or more complicated architectures.

item.title: Symmetry-adapted perturbation theory for cavity-modified intermolecular interactions: QED-SAPT0 theory and implementation
item.description: We develop a cavity quantum electrodynamics symmetry adapted perturbation theory (QED-SAPT) formalism that directly models intermolecular interactions in quantized cavity environments. By formulating the zeroth-order problem in a coherent state basis, we define the inter-monomer perturbation as the sum of the standard Coulombic contribution and an inter-monomer dipole self energy contribution. This yields a particularly convenient structure whereby the new inter-monomer cavity components can be incorporated through a simple augmentation of the dressed integrals that arise in standard SAPT theory. We also leverage this structure in a density fitted implementation and demonstrate the performance advantage over an implementation that utilizes the full electron integral tensor. Finally, we utilize this formalism to explore several representative molecular clusters from the S66 data set and provide comparison to QED-CCSD and QED-DFT formalisms.

item.title: Mineralisation behaviour during heterogeneous photo-Fenton treatment of amoxicillin in a rotating Fe2O3-impregnated disc reactor: the controlling role of oxidant stoichiometry
item.description: Conventional biological treatment does not remove antibiotic residues, and in Jordan this matters more than in most places, because reclaimed effluent supplies a large share of the water used for irrigation. Heterogeneous photo-Fenton treatment is one candidate for a tertiary polishing step: the iron stays on a recoverable support, so the process avoids the sludge that homogeneous Fenton chemistry produces. We treated amoxicillin (AMX) in a closed 1 L rotating catalytic disc reactor holding ten Fe2O3-impregnated mesh discs (0.435 mmol Fe g-1; 93 g in total), irradiated by three UV-C lamps at 254 nm and turned at about 20 rpm. Seven runs were carried out at 100, 500 and 1000 mg L-1 AMX and pH ≈ 3, at peroxide doses of roughly 140 µL and 1.0 mL, and followed by total carbon (TC) or non-purgeable organic carbon (NPOC) for up to 17 h. Peroxide is consumed by every route that makes a hydroxyl radical, and 35 mol of it are needed per mol of AMX for complete mineralisation. The fractional carbon removal a run can achieve is therefore capped by the fraction f of that demand actually supplied. Our doses gave f = 1.4–20.4%, so complete mineralisation was unattainable before the experiments began. Every apparent carbon removal nevertheless exceeded its cap, in one case by a factor of 13.6, and cannot therefore be attributed to mineralisation. The carbon increases of up to 87.6% cannot be attributed to intermediates either, since fragmentation redistributes carbon without generating it. What the reactor can achieve, and how its carbon data should be read, are both governed by oxidant stoichiometry rather than by catalyst loading or irradiation time.

item.title: High-Resolution MRT-TOF Mass Spectrometry Enables Simultaneous Carbon and Nitrogen Tracing in Stable Isotope Resolved Metabolomics
item.description: Stable isotope-resolved metabolomics (SIRM) using dual-isotope tracers, such as [U-13C5,15N2]glutamine, provides complementary insight into carbon and nitrogen metabolism and their integration across interconnected metabolic pathways. However, distinguishing closely spaced 13C- and 15N-containing isotopologues requires resolving power that conventional quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometers (QTOF MS) may not provide. In this study, we evaluated the performance of a multi-reflecting time-of-flight (MRT) mass spectrometer for dual-isotope SIRM using [U-13C5,15N2]glutamine-infused patient-derived tumor xenografts and compared its performance with that of a conventional SYNAPT™ XS QTOF Platform operated at a resolving power of approximately 15,000. A total of 113 metabolites were detected on both platforms, and dual-isotope labeling patterns were evaluated for 29 carbon- and nitrogen-containing metabolites. The Xevo™ MRT Mass Spectrometer, operating at a resolving power of approximately 100,000, resolved closely spaced 13C- and 15N isotopologues that remained unresolved on the SYNAPT™ XS Instrument under the acquisition conditions used. This separation enabled composition-specific isotopologue assignment, independent peak integration, natural-abundance correction, and isotopologue-specific fractional-enrichment analysis. The higher sensitivity of Xevo™ MRT Mass Spectrometer improved detection of low-abundance isotopologues, increasing isotopologue coverage when compared to SYNAPT™ XS MS Instrument. Together, these results demonstrate that MRT-TOF mass spectrometry provides a practical high-resolution platform for dual-isotope SIRM and enables simultaneous assessment of carbon incorporation and nitrogen-transfer reactions within a single experiment.

item.title: From Notch-Tip Stress to Mechanophore Activation - A Multiscale Study of Mechanochromic PMMA
item.description: Mechanophore-functionalized polymers enable optical readout of molecular-level stress under macroscopic deformation. Spiropyran (SP)-doped poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) provides a well-established platform for mechanochemical stress sensing, yet molecular stress fields around defined geometric stress concentrators remain largely disconnected from continuum mechanics. To bridge this gap, we develop a geometry-matched molecular dynamics (MD) and finite-element (FE) approach for PMMA containing two opposing semi-elliptical notches of systematically varied depth and width. Molecular simulations employ a hybrid coarse-grained/all-atom (CG/AA) PMMA model with atomistically resolved, quantum-chemically (QC) informed SP, while the FE models use the MD-derived stress–strain response of bulk PMMA as input. Under uniaxial tension, both approaches capture notch-tip stress localization, plastic-zone propagation toward the ligament center, and the characteristic butterfly-shaped stress field. FE simulations reproduce MD notch-tip stresses, demonstrating that suitably parameterized continuum models capture key notch mechanics, whereas defect-mediated rearrangements require molecular resolution. Notch geometry strongly enhances SP activation to its merocyanine (MC) form, lowering the onset strain and localizing activation in highly elongated chains and around deformation-induced voids near the notch edges. These results link defect geometry and molecular stress concentration to mechanophore activation and directly connect molecular and continuum notch mechanics.

item.title: TAPERSS-MoCa: A Physics-Based Monte Carlo Framework for 3D RNA Structure Prediction from Sequence
item.description: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) function is intrinsically linked to its three-dimensional architecture, yet experimental structure determination remains challenging. Here, we introduce TAPERSS-MoCa (Theoretical Analyses, Prediction, and Evaluation of RNA Structures from Sequence using a Monte-Carlo Simulator), a physics-based fragment assembly framework for predicting RNA tertiary structures directly from sequence. By utilizing a novel fragment library grounded in dinucleoside monophosphate (DNMP) energetics parameterized via Discrete Path Sampling (DPS), TAPERSS-MoCa efficiently samples low-energy conformational landscapes. Evaluated across 6-, 10-, and 12-nucleotide RNA test sets, TAPERSS-MoCa consistently recovers native-like global minima with canonical Watson–Crick base pairs adopting near-planar geometry. By combining dinucleoside fragment energetics with an angularly constrained hydrogen-bonding potential, TAPERSS-MoCa accurately captures A-form structures in 6-nucleotide linear RNAs, outperforming traditional fragment-assembly algorithms that frequently misfold these flexible sequences. Thermodynamic evaluations based on ensemble partition functions (ΔGfolding) and macrostate basin free energies (ΔFfolding) demonstrate strong predictive performance for rigid, well-stacked GNRA tetraloops. Furthermore, TAPERSS-MoCa systematically reproduces key physical stability trends predicted by empirical nearest-neighbor models. This physics-based approach provides a robust platform for structural prediction and thermodynamic profiling of short RNA motifs, supporting RNA-targeted drug discovery and functional design.

item.title: Programmable Formic Acid Decomposition in Flow on an Interdigitated Internal Catalytic Condenser Beyond the Sabatier Limit
Breaking the Potency Barrier: A Practical Recipe for QSAR Extrapolation
item.description: Predicting compounds that are more potent than those represented in the training data remains a difficult and practically important problem for quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) modeling. This challenge is particularly relevant during lead optimization, where the goal is to design or identify analogs that are more potent than compounds already measured. To address this problem, we developed a new Pairwise-Difference QSAR (PD-QSAR) approach that learns changes in biological activity from differences in molecular descriptors between compound pairs. We evaluated three strategies for aggregating the resulting PD-QSAR predictions: mean aggregation, k-nearest-neighbor aggregation (k = 3), and 10% quantile aggregation, and compared their performance with Direct QSAR and Chemprop using a benchmark derived from publicly available ChEMBL 35 data. The primary benchmark included 103 human single-protein target datasets, comprising 33,707 activity records. For each target, the 10% most potent activity records were withheld for external validation. Among the approaches evaluated, 10% quantile aggregation provided the lowest median external validation RMSE (0.518) and outperformed mean and kNN aggregation on external validation RMSE for 100 of 103 targets, Direct QSAR for 102 targets, and Chemprop for 94 targets. These results support PD-QSAR with quantile aggregation as a useful strategy for prioritizing analogs expected to extend beyond the potency range represented by previously measured compounds.

item.title: Directional Electric Fields at Designed MOF Sites: Implications for Electrostatic Preorganization and Catalysis
item.description: Enzymes achieve their enormous catalytic power in part through electrostatic preorganization: non-covalent interactions arrange an electric field that is preorganized to stabilize the change in dipole moment between a reaction's ground and transition states. Thus, the catalytic relevance of an electric field depends not only on its magnitude but also on its orientation. Here we use the enforced rigidity of a metal–organic framework (MOF), PCN-521, to demonstrate this orientation dependence directly. We introduce an aldehyde carbonyl vibrational Stark probe in situ, first as a protected ketal, then deprotect it to reveal a carbonyl at the same node-capping site as a previously reported nitrile probe, extending field measurements to a field reporter of greater relevance to enzymatic catalysis. Electric field- vibrational frequency calibrated probes using the vibrational Stark effect report a trifluoroacetate field donor that projects nearly its full destabilizing field onto the collinear nitrile (sp, C≡N) but only a fraction onto the off-axis aldehyde (sp2, C=O) — a geometric effect. Because the framework's non-covalent contacts, unlike an enzyme active site's, cannot reorganize, this controlled, single-site comparison isolates alignment from magnitude. While electric fields are often invoked to explain observations near electrodes or droplet interfaces, these results show the importance of alignment which is often neglected.

item.title: Geometrical Constraints Weaken a Nickel–Hydrogen Bond and Enable the Homolytic H2 Evolution Mechanism
item.description: Mechanistic studies of the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) are helping advance catalysis towards energy storage technologies based on water splitting. Homolytic H–H bondforming pathways are one of the fundamental mechanisms of HER, yet well-defined examples of bimetallic coupling in molecular HER catalysts remain extremely rare. A planar tetradentate bipyridine diphosphinite ligand (PONNOP) is reported that constrains the geometry of nickel complexes, weakening the Ni–H bond dissociation free energy and enabling H2 evolution via the homolytic pathway. Crystallography, magnetism, absorption spectroscopy, and computational studies provide insight into the electronic structure enforced by the rigid tetradentate PONNOP ligand, which results in a very weak Ni–H bond in a transiently formed metal hydride. Cyclic voltammetry and chronoamperometry studies are consistent with electrocatalytic HER via the homolytic mechanism. The ability of a tetradentate ligand to induce M–H bond-weakening is discussed as a possible design element in HER by Earth-abundant catalysts.

item.title: Machine Learning Identifies an Information-Sufficiency Regime for Critical-Mineral Recovery
item.description: The recovery of critical minerals from spent lithium-ion batteries is governed by coupled feedstock chemistry, solvent composition, and processing conditions, yet heterogeneous experimental reporting makes it difficult to determine which information is essential for reliable prediction across heterogeneous experimental systems. Here, using deep eutectic solvent-based recovery as a representative resource recovery platform, we curate 814 experimental observations from 38 publications and develop an interpretable machine learning framework to identify an informationsufficiency regime. Five descriptors, including temperature, electrode material type, leaching time, target metal, and hydrogen-bond donor identity, retain 98.3% of the predictive performance of the full 13-descriptor model while reducing the descriptor space by 61.5%. Reducing the representation from five to four descriptors causes a pronounced performance loss, whereas adding a sixth provides negligible additional benefit. Descriptor removal and domain ablation analyses further show that temperature and target metal identity contain the least replaceable predictive information, while material identity, solvent chemistry, and processing conditions provide complementary information. These results identify a compact, chemically structured information core for critical-mineral recovery and provide a quantitative basis for prioritizing experimental measurements, improving cross-study data consistency, and developing more transferable datadriven frameworks for battery resource recovery.

item.title: An Annotation Consistency Checker for Evidence-Based Evaluation of Untargeted LC-MS/MS Metabolite Annotations
item.description: Untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics routinely produces complex annotation landscapes in which individual spectra can yield multiple candidate metabolite annotations. Although spectral similarity provides an essential foundation for library-based annotation, determining whether a candidate annotation is consistent with the available evidence and whether alternative explanations remain plausible requires integration of multiple lines of evidence. In current practice, this evaluation is largely embedded in expert judgment, making annotation review difficult to teach, standardize, and reproduce. Here, we introduce an annotation consistency checker that aids this expert review process by generating a user-inspectable report for spectral library matches. The framework integrates complementary evidence dimensions, including spectral agreement, structural relationships among candidate annotations, and competing library matches to highlight annotations that are supported by, or inconsistent with, the available data. Biological context is provided separately to aid interpretation of metabolite occurrence across organisms, tissues, and sample types but is not incorporated into the annotation score. By enabling systematic evaluation of multiple evidence streams, this approach provides a transparent workflow that helps users critically assess metabolite annotations, reduce overinterpretation of spectral matches, and make informed decisions beyond only accepting the top-ranked library match.

item.title: (ImRN)2Fe: An Elusive Complex and the Limits of Its Ferrocene Analogy
item.description: The isolobal relationship between imidazolin-2-iminato and cyclopentadienyl ligands makes the iron bis(imidazolin-2-iminato) complex (ImRN)2Fe an attractive target as a potential ferrocene analog, yet reported efforts toward its isolation have been unsuccessful. Herein, we report the synthesis of (ImDippN)2Fe (1) by protonolysis of Fe2Mes4 with ImDippNH, affording a linear, two-coordinate, high-spin Fe(II) complex (S = 2). Its coordinative unsaturation permits binding of THF, an aryl isocyanide, and TEMPO, affording complexes with varied geometries. Unlike ferrocene, the electrochemical properties of 1 depend strongly on its ancillary ligands. Oxidation with AgPF6 affords a Ag-bound Fe(II) intermediate 1-Ag that undergoes photochemical conversion to the Fe(III) complex [(ImDippN)2Fe(Solv)2][PF6] (2). These results establish 1 as a distinct low-coordinate iron complex whose coordination and redox chemistry extend beyond its proposed ferrocene analogy.

item.title: Growth-Triggered Nano-vesicle Budding via Leaflet Area Asymmetry in Fatty-Acid Protocells
item.description: CORRECTION NOTICE (version 2). Three results reported in version 1 do not survive a more careful treatment of the bud geometry, and a one-page correction notice has been prepended to the document; the original text follows it unaltered. (1) The self-consistency condition x_extra = 0 of Sec. 2.3 describes a bud drawn from the outer leaflet alone. A closed vesicle has two leaflets, and matching the removed areas to those of a closed spherical bud fixes x_extra at about -2 for every radius between 60 nm and 1 micrometre, so no non-negative value is admissible. (2) The predicted bud radius of 60-90 nm therefore does not follow. It came from equating the excess outer-leaflet area with the bud's total area; a closed bud instead withdraws 8 pi h r of area difference, giving r = R x Delta a_c, which is 500 nm to 1 micrometre for a parent of 1 micrometre. The corrected behaviour is growth followed by division-scale budding rather than sustained growth punctuated by nano-shedding. (3) The reduced imbalance Delta a used here counts the excess accumulated during growth, whereas the O(1) criterion quoted from the area-difference-elasticity literature is stated in the normalisation where a sphere already carries unit reduced area difference; the two are related by Delta a_ADE = 1 + Delta a. The kinetic scheme and its steady state are unaffected, as is the qualitative prediction that shed vesicles are enriched in recently inserted material. Derivations are given in doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15010117/v3. ORIGINAL ABSTRACT (version 1). Fatty-acid vesicles growing by monomer uptake, as demonstrated experimentally for Szostak-type protocells, insert new amphiphiles predominantly into the outer leaflet. Because transbilayer flip-flop is not instantaneous, this generates a growing area mismatch between the two leaflets. We show, using the area-difference-elasticity (ADE) framework for vesicle shape, that this mismatch crosses a threshold beyond which the vesicle relieves it by shedding small, high-curvature nano-vesicles rather than by symmetric division – with no external mechanical forcing required. A leaflet-resolved kinetic model shows that sustained parent growth over many such cycles requires the shed nano-vesicles to be compositionally enriched in the destabilizing (outer-leaflet) material rather than ordinary bilayer: a specific, falsifiable prediction. For illustrative growth and flip-flop rates the model predicts nano-vesicles of radius 60–90 nm, above the stability floor of fatty-acid vesicles. This mechanism, and its central prediction, match independent experimental observations on fatty-acid and lysolipid-containing vesicles. In an earlier work [1] we explored periodic environmental mechanical forcing (tidal, geyser and vortex-driven shear) as an alternative trigger for vesicle instability; that mechanism rests on poorly constrained assumptions about Hadean orbital dynamics and produces, in its simplest form, no resonance, only a low-pass response. The present mechanism requires no assumption about the early Earth’s mechanical environment at all.

item.title: Tension-Limited Leaflet-Asymmetry Budding Predicts the Size and Rate of Tumour Ectosome Shedding
item.description: Fatty-acid protocells growing by outer-leaflet monomer uptake accumulate a transbilayer area imbalance that is relieved by budding once the reduced imbalance Δa exceeds a critical value, as described by area-difference elasticity (ADE). It is tempting to read modern tumour ectosome shedding as the same physics. We show that the naive transfer fails, and derive the version that does not. A protocell is osmotically relaxed; the plasma membrane of a cancer cell is under tension (σ ≈ 0.01–0.1 mN/m), which imposes an area cost absent from the protocell treatment. Replacing the shape-instability criterion with an explicit energy balance for bud formation gives a threshold in the differential leaflet tension, Δτ_c = sqrt(8κΣ)/h with Σ = σ + K_A h^2/R^2, and a bud radius at threshold r* = sqrt(2κ/Σ) that is independent of both h and K_A. Retaining the finite-parent term K_A h^2/R^2 is essential: in the tension-free limit it acts as an effective tension, so the threshold does not vanish but tends to Δa_c → sqrt(2κ/K_A)/h = 0.21–0.87, equivalently 1.21–1.87 in the convention where a sphere carries unit reduced area difference. The O(1) ADE criterion assumed for protocells is thereby recovered as a derived result. The stored imbalance at threshold pays for exactly 1 + R^2 σ/(K_A h^2) buds, independent of κ: one for a tension-free vesicle, which therefore divides, and 11-2600 for a tense plasma membrane, which sheds a burst of nano-vesicles. The protocell growth kinetics map exactly onto flippase/scramblase imbalance under γ → 2a_L j. Using bending rigidities measured on giant plasma membrane vesicles (κ = 5.4–35 k_BT, including the metastatic line MDA-MB-231), the model predicts bud diameters of 43–346 nm, overlapping measured cancer extracellular vesicles, at a threshold requiring translocation of only 0.09–0.76 mol% of plasma-membrane lipid. Because a single TMEM16F scramblase translocates 45 000 lipids per second while the critical net flux is below one lipid per second per square micron, the thermodynamic threshold is not the regulated quantity: the shedding rate is. Reported secretion rates of 60–80 EV per cell per hour correspond to a net outward flux of 0.2–1 lipid per square micrometre per second, a calibration rather than a test of the model. Two falsification tests on the threshold locus, to which shedding pins the membrane — the bud radius falls as the inverse square root of the membrane tension, and grows as the square root of the bending rigidity — distinguish this mechanism from ESCRT-dependent biogenesis. We argue explicitly against reading the size agreement between protocells and tumour vesicles as evolutionary atavism.

item.title: Methodology for Fabricating and Testing Carbon Molecular Sieve (CMS) Dense Film Membranes for Reproducible Permeation Experiments
item.description: Carbon molecular sieve (CMS) membranes are promising for demanding gas separations, but their brittleness after pyrolysis makes dense-film permeation testing difficult and often irreproducible. Membranes that appear defect-free after pyrolysis can crack during handling, masking, permeation cell assembly, vacuum evacuation or gas pressurization. This work presents a practical procedure for fabricating and testing CMS dense films prepared from fluorinated polyimide-based CMS membranes. We investigated several experimental factors such as polymer concentration, membrane casting in glove bag, epoxy selection, filter paper support, masking and pressure loading, and their resulting impact on the mechanical stability of the membranes Careful control of these steps reduced or entirely mitigated film cracking, gas bypass during testing, and epoxy seal failure during permeation measurements. This study provides a reliable method for casting, masking and testing of fragile CMS dense film membranes and addresses practical details that are often not reported, but are important for successful and reproducible gas permeation data with CMS membranes.

item.title: Whole-Enzyme Reactive Free-Energy Simulations with a Universal Machine Learning Interatomic Potential: Catalytic Mechanism and Mutational Effects of PETase
item.description: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) have emerged as powerful tools for atomistic simulations that achieve quantum mechanical accuracy at significantly reduced computational cost. Yet, their direct application to complex enzymatic reactions remains challenging owing to the immense size of solvated enzyme systems and the scarcity of transition-state structures in training data. In this study, we demonstrate that PFP (PreFerred Potential), a pretrained uMLIP across 96 elements in nature, simulates the complete hydrolytic cycle of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) catalyzed by PETase as a single reactive domain of approximately 20,000 atoms, without multiscale partitioning or system-specific fine-tuning. Umbrella-sampling simulations revealed stepwise mechanisms for both acylation and deacylation through distinct tetrahedral intermediates. The computed rate-limiting deacylation barrier of 20.5 ± 0.3 kcal/mol is in agreement with the range of 18.0–18.7 kcal/mol inferred from experimental turnover numbers. The PFP-based simulations further capture catalytic consequences of point mutations from loss of function (D177N, M132A) to predicted activity enhancement (D157N) and reveal that simultaneous neutralization of three distal acidic residues which are located more than 10 Å from the active site raises the activation barrier due to a collective long-range electrostatic effect that emerges naturally in the partition-free treatment. These findings demonstrate that the pretrained uMLIP, PFP, can provide physically plausible free-energy profiles for enzymatic reaction mechanisms and capture mutational effects, providing a powerful platform for rational enzyme design.

item.title: Correlative Analysis of Individual Suspended Photocatalyst Particles Enabled by Optical Particle Trapping with Electrochemical Sensing
item.description: In particulate photocatalysis, typical experiments involve billions to trillions of particles that possess highly heterogeneous properties, making it difficult to uncover mechanisms and structure-property relationships at the single-particle level. Additionally, existing single-particle measurement techniques become limited by the need to anchor particles to substrates and lack the ability to control interparticle spacing and interactions. Herein, we describe a multi-modal technique called optical particle trapping with electrochemical sensing (OPTECS), whereby the distributions of product generation rates from fully wetted, individual photocatalyst particles are measured using microelectrode sensors while simultaneously recording their luminescent characteristics. Using doped bismuth vanadate and strontium titanate as model particulate photocatalysts towards overall water splitting, OPTECS is used to reveal (i) hidden correlations between single particle luminescence intensity and photoactivity, and (ii) the presence of optically stimulated electrochemiluminescence (OSECL), which is leveraged to quantify rates of undesired back reactions, a key loss mechanism in particulate photocatalysis.

item.title: Photocatalytic dehydrogenation enables divergent access to functional polyolefins
item.description: Polyolefins are among the most widely used plastics, yet their chemically inert hydrocarbon backbones severely limit opportunities for chemical modification and value-added reuse. Introducing carbon–carbon double bonds offers a powerful way to transform these otherwise unreactive materials into versatile intermediates for downstream chemistry. Here we report an acceptorless photocatalytic/cobalt-catalyzed dehydrogenation that operates across a broad range of polyethylene- and polypropylene-based materials, including post-consumer plastics. Notably, polypropylene undergoes dehydrogenation with near-exclusive selectivity for terminal alkene formation. The resulting unsaturated polyolefins serve as versatile platforms for diverse transformations, enabling access to functionalized polyolefins, telechelic polyethylene, as well as block and graft copolymers. These products further demonstrate utility as compatibilizers for immiscible polymer blends and as strong adhesive materials. By converting inert C–H backbones into chemically addressable alkene-containing polymers, this strategy transforms commodity polyolefins into diverse polymer architectures with practical functions.

item.title: Nonadiabatic Semiclassical Polariton Dynamics: Excited State Proton Transfer of Aminopropenal
item.description: The interplay between strong light-matter coupling and nonadiabatic molecular dynamics provides a promising route to control chemical reactivity. Here, we develop a framework for simulating polaritonic chemistry with on-the-fly semiclassical nonadiabatic molecular dynamics, employing the linearized semiclassical initial value representation. With this approach, we simulate the nonadiabatic molecular dynamics under strong light-matter coupling, presenting results for excited state proton transfer of aminopropenal. Light-matter interactions are described using a Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian formulated in the adiabatic electronic basis, where the electronic energies, transition moments, and nuclear forces are evaluated on the fly.
